title: Do Speak, We would Listen...
paragraphs: Is the word ilakkiyam of Tamil origin? Or does it belong to the Sanskrit language? This was the topic of a big debate.

This issue necessitated more or less a forum for debate. It came up in the function on Muttamiḻ (Threefold Tamil) organised in May 1949 at Coimbatore. Pāvēntar Pāratitācaṉ presided over the function. I was also present at the function in which Ariñar Aṇṇā, Avvai Duraisamy Piḷḷai, the multilingual scholar Appadurai, the great critic Veḷḷaivāraṇar and many others participated.
Hardly was there any discourse on the development of Tamil or the rise of the Tamils.
In the huge gathering of ten thousand people, the only question that dominated the proceedings was ‘Is ilakkiyam a Tamil word or not?’
Speaking on the second day, I observed thus:

“Having mobilized ten thousand people and spent thousands of rupees to conduct this function to which renowned scholars and academics are invited, you have wasted two days’ time and deliberations by focusing upon the single issue of deciding as to whether ilakkiyam is a Tamil word or not. Instead, a group of eight or ten of these scholars could have assembled in a separate place and done this
research. One of these scholars then could have conveyed to us the result of your deliberations.”

My speech created a big sensation. I referred to this Muttamiḻ Viḻā function to drive home the point that the debate as to whether ilakkiyam is derived from ilaṭciyam (objective) or from ilaṅkutal (shine forth as an example) still continues. We have such a debate in Tolkāppiyam also:
> Usage > Being the word of the learned, > Propriety in poetry > Draws on conformity to the usage.
Iḷampūraṇar’s commentary on this verse is that poetic diction should adopt the usage that comes to be the standard from the use of the learned.

Nacciṉārkkiṉiyar, on the other hand, adds the conjunctive particle um to uyarntōr kiḷavi (the usage of the learned) and says that the learned usage going in accord with the vedic usage becomes the poetic diction.
Here, the word vaḻakku (usage) does not refer to any case filed in a court of law! Instead, it refers to usage of words and sentences.
Iḷampūraṇar claims that only the words of learned men can become the standard of usage.
The conjunctive particle of Nacciṉārkkiṉiyar may imply that there exists iḻintōr kiḷavi (the diction of the lowly) too, which goes against the norm in Tolkāppiyam Marapiyal section that
> Usage is > What is in vogue and use > Among the learned.
Quoting this in his Tolkāppiyam commentary, the great Tamil scholar Veḷḷaivāraṇar points out that vaḻakku (usage) is linguistic usage, and reference to vedic usage is out of place.
Another commentator Pērāciriyar agreeing with Iḷampūraṇar says that usage is the use of language by the learned because it is from that the events of popular speech issue.
The use of the lowly, such as
> eṉṉaṭā tapāykkiṟē (What man, trying to escape?) > eṉṉammā moṟaikkiṟē (You woman! Why staring at me?)
can never become norms of usage.
> Usage > Being the word of the learned, > Propriety in poetry > Draws on conformity to the usage.
(Poruḷatikāram : Poruḷiyal, verse 23)
